overview.body:
**Hrungnir** ​(*hrungnir*) — ‌Giant, Duel ‌with Thor ​· ​Brawler — ​belongs to ​the Norse ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Giant, Duel ‌with Thor". ​The name ‌means ​"Brawler"[^1].

Hrungnir ​is the ​strongest of ​the ​jötnar — ‌the stone-hearted ​giant who ‌rode ​his gold-maned ‌stallion Gullfaxi ​into Ásgarðr ‌on ​a wager ‌of heads, ​drank Thor's ​liquor ‌from the ‌god's own ‌horns, boasted ​he ​would carry ‌off Valhǫll, ​and met ​Mjǫllnir ‌at Grjótúnagarðar ​with nothing ​in his ‌hand ​but a ‌whetstone. His ​duel is ​the ​most fully ​narrated single ‌combat between ‌god ​and giant ‌in the ​Old Norse ​corpus.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Hrungnir** ‌and ​serves its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/hrungnir/). ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form — ​a description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*hrungnir* survives ​as a ‌modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.
Þjóðólfr of Hvin, Haustlöng (the shield-poem's account of the Hrungnir combat, quoted in Skáldskaparmál).
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. Hrungnir, Gullfaxi, Grjótúnagarðar, hein.

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Younger ​Futhark ​as **ᚼᚱᚢᚾᚴᚾᛁᚱ**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"Brawler"[^1].

The ​ASCII ‌form ​*hrungnir* survives ‌only ​because ‌the ​early domain-name ​system ​could ​not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration ​**Hrungnir** ‌recovers the ‌full ‌diacritic ​detail of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​directly in ‌the ​address ​bar. ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— ​a description ​computed ​from ‌the ‌displayed form ​itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**h** ‌→ ‌**H** — ‌Same
- ​**r** ‌→ ​**r** — ​Same
- ​**u** ‌→ ​**u** — ​Same
- ​**n** ‌→ ​**n** — ​Same
- ​**g** ‌→ ​**g** — ‌Same
- ​**n** ‌→ **n** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**i** ​→ **i** ​— ​Same
- ​**r** ‌→ **r** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈhruŋɡ.nir/** — ‌Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

- ​**Hr-** — Aspirate [h] ​running straight into ​the trilled [r] ​— an initial cluster ‌Old Norse kept ​but English dropped, ​as in hringr ‌'ring' versus its silent-h ​descendants.
- **-u-** — ‌Short close back ​rounded [u], the vowel ‌of 'put', held ​brief between the ​r and the ​nasal.
- **-ng-** — Velar ​nasal [ŋ] plus ​a fully sounded ‌stop [g] — Old ​Norse sounded both, ‌as in English ​'finger', never the bare ‌nasal of 'singer'.
- ​**-nir** — Second ‌[n], short [i], ​and the final nominative ‌-r, lightly trilled ​— the masculine ​agent ending that marks ‌him as a ‌doer.

For the ‌modern speaker, the ​closest approximation is: 'HRUNG-nir' ​— begin with ‌a breathy h, ​roll the r straight ​into a short ‌'oo' as in ​'put', sound both the ​ng and the ‌g as in ​'finger', and trill ‌the final r.

Kindred ​and historical forms ​of the name:

- ​**Old Norse** — Hrungnir, ​the strongest of ‌the jötnar; no ‌secure cognate or agreed ​etymology survives in ‌the handbooks.
- **Younger ​Futhark** — ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ ​(h-r-u-k-n-i-R), the Viking-Age carving ‌of the name; ‌ᚴ writes both ‌k and g, and ‌ᛦ the final ​nominative -r.
- **Skaldic ‌attestation** — Hrungnir, ​named and fought in ​Þjóðólfr of Hvin's ​Haustlöng (early 10th ‌c.), the oldest sustained ​witness to the ​duel.

Hrungnir is ​a plain restoration by ‌the mechanical rule: ​the normalized Old ​Norse form is ​already plain ASCII — ‌no diacritic, no ​distinctive letter — ‌so the restoration preserves ​nothing the ASCII ‌form loses. The ​name's obscurity is ‌a statement about etymology, ‌never about the ​giant: the handbooks ​register Hrungnir's origin as ​uncertain while his ​duel with Þórr ‌is among the best-attested ‌single combats in ​the corpus.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger Futhark ​as ​**ᚼᚱᚢᚾᚴᚾᛁᚱ**.[^1]

The ​scholarly transliteration ​is ​*hrunknir*.

The ‌rendering proceeds ​step by ​step:

- ‌ᚼ (hagall) ​writes /h/
- ‌ᚱ (reið) ​writes ‌/r/
- ᚢ ​(úr) writes ​the ​rounded back ​vowels /u, ​o, ø, ‌ǫ, ​y/ and ‌/w/
- The ​spelling hrunknir ‌is ​a normalized ‌phonetic reconstruction; ​Younger ‌Futhark does ​not distinguish ​voiced/voiceless stops ‌or ‌separate short ‌and long ​vowels

The ​normalized ‌Old Norse ​form is ​**Hrungnir** ‌— already ​plain ASCII, ​with no ‌diacritic ​or distinctive ‌letter for ​the restoration ​to ​recover; in ​the Younger ‌Futhark ‌the name ​would have ‌been carved ​ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ ​(h-r-u-k-n-i-R, the ‌ᚴ-rune writing ‌g and ‌ᛦ ‌the final ​nominative -r). ‌Because ​the name ​is pure ​ASCII, its ‌domain ​was registered ​in the ​ordinary way ‌long ​ago: **hrungnir.com ​is held ​by ‌a third ​party outside ‌the PuniCodex ​collection ‌and is ​watched for ‌release** — ‌no ​form of ​the name ​is ​currently owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

sources.citation: An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. with supplement, 1874.
Poetic Edda (Eddukvæði), ed. Neckel-Kuhn; trans. Carolyn Larrington, Oxford World's Classics (2014), 1270.
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, trans. Anthony Faulkes, Everyman / Viking Society for Northern Research, 1220.
A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, Oxford, 1910.

domains.body:
Hrungnir ​is the ‌strongest of ‌the jötnar ​— the ​stone-hearted giant ​who rode ​his gold-maned ​stallion Gullfaxi ‌into ​Ásgarðr on ​a wager ‌of heads, ​drank Thor's ‌liquor from ​the god's ‌own horns, ​boasted he ​would ​carry off ​Valhǫll, and ​met Mjǫllnir ‌at Grjótúnagarðar ​with nothing ‌in his ​hand but ‌a ​whetstone. His ‌duel is ​the most ‌fully narrated ​single combat ​between god ‌and giant ‌in the ‌Old ​Norse corpus.[^1]

### ​Gullfaxi

'Golden ‌mane' — ​the stallion ​Óðinn envied ‌aloud, whose ​speed Hrungnir ​wagered his ‌head ​against Sleipnir ‌to disprove.

### ​The Whetstone

​His weapon ​of stone ​— hurled ‌against Mjǫllnir, ‌it shattered ​in ‌mid-air; one ​shard fathered ​every whetstone ‌rock on ‌earth, one ‌lodged in ‌Thor's skull.

### ​The Stone ‌Heart

​Three-cornered, sharp-edged, ​and hard ​— the ‌Edda says ​his heart, ​head, and ​shield were ‌all ​of stone, ​a giant ​made of ‌his own ​weapon's material.

### ‌Grjótúnagarðar

The ​'stone-fence-yard' at ‌the edge ​of ‌heaven and ‌giantland, where ​the single ​combat was ​appointed — ​the oldest ‌named duelling-ground ‌in the ​myths.

sources.citation: Þjóðólfr of Hvin, Haustlöng (the shield-poem's account of the Hrungnir combat, quoted in Skáldskaparmál).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Hrungnir concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of recurring ​attributes, ‌each a ​compressed ​statement ‌about the ​name:[^1]

- ‌**The whetstone** ​— ‌The honing-stone ​hurled ​against the ​hammer ​— stone ​against ‌iron, and ​the ‌shard still ​buried ‌in Thor's ​head
- ‌**Gullfaxi** — ​The ‌gold-maned stallion ​whose ​speed was ‌worth ‌a ‌giant's head ​— ​and ended ‌in ​the hands ​of ‌three-night-old Magni
- ​**The ​three-cornered stone ‌heart** ​— Courage ‌of ​the wrong ​material: ​resolve that ​is ‌hard, sharp, ‌and ​entirely without ‌flexibility
- ​**Mǫkkurkálfi** ​— The ‌nine-league ‌clay giant ‌with ‌a mare's ​heart ‌— the ​giants' ​engineered champion, ​terror ‌to look ​at ​and nothing ​within
- ‌**The fallen ​foot** ​— Hrungnir's ​leg ‌across Thor's ​neck, ‌which all ​the ‌Æsir ​together could ‌not ‌lift — ​the ​weight of ​the ​foe after ‌the ‌foe is ​dead

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

mythology.body:
Hrungnir has essentially one story, and ​it is the greatest fight in the Edda: the wager, ‌the drunken boasting in the hall of the gods, the appointed ‌duel at Grjótúnagarðar, the shattered whetstone, and the fall that left ​even victorious Thor pinned beneath his enemy's leg. Snorri tells ​it in Skáldskaparmál, and the skald Þjóðólfr of Hvin had carved ​it into verse three centuries earlier.[^1]

### The Wager of Heads ​(Skáldskaparmál 17)

It begins with a boast Óðinn could not keep ​to himself. Riding Sleipnir through Jötunheimr, he met the giant Hrungnir, ‌who asked who this man was with the golden helmet, ​riding so well over sea and air, and praised the horse. ​Óðinn answered with the stake that decides everything after: he ‌wagered his head that no horse in Jötunheimr was Sleipnir's equal. ​Hrungnir sprang to his own stallion Gullfaxi, the gold-maned, and gave ‌chase in a fury. The race ran to the very ​gates of Ásgarðr — and Hrungnir, carried past his own turning, ‌galloped through them and in among the gods.[^2]

### Drunk in ​the Hall of the Gods (Skáldskaparmál 17)

The Æsir received him ​with the hospitality due an uninvited guest: they set before him ​the great horns Thor himself drank from, and Hrungnir emptied ​them one after another. Drunk, he let the boasts out — ​he would take Valhǫll up and carry it off to ‌Jötunheimr, he would sink Ásgarðr, he would kill all the gods, ​save only Freyja and Sif, whom he would carry home; and ‌the mead, he said, he would drink up all by ​himself. The Æsir, tired of the noise, named Thor; and Thor ‌came in swinging his hammer, demanding who had given jötnar ​leave to drink in Valhǫll. Hrungnir, looking at him with anything ‌but friendly eyes, answered that Óðinn had invited him and he ​stood under Óðinn's protection — then claimed his rights: Thor ‌would gain little honour from killing him unarmed. It would be ​a greater trial of courage, he said, if Thor dared ​meet him in single combat at the frontier, at Grjótúnagarðar. And ‌Thor, Snorri says, would by no means refuse a challenge to ‌single combat.

### Grjótúnagarðar: The Whetstone and the Hammer (Skáldskaparmál 17–19)

‌The giants made much of the appointment, for Hrungnir was the ​strongest of them and they expected one outcome or the ​other to be decisive. For his second they built a champion ‌of clay: Mǫkkurkálfi, nine leagues tall and three leagues broad across ​the chest, with no heart big enough for the frame ​— so they gave him a mare's heart, and it quaked ‌within him when Thor came. Hrungnir stood with his heart ​of stone, three-cornered and sharp-edged, his head of stone, and his ​broad shield of stone, holding his hone — the whetstone — ‌before him. Þjálfi ran ahead and called out that Thor ​was coming from below, and Hrungnir, fearing a strike through the ‌earth, set the shield beneath his feet and stood on it.

​Then Thor came in an ásmegin-fury, lightning running before him, ​and hurled Mjǫllnir from afar. Hrungnir threw the hone with both ​hands, and the weapons met in the air. The hone ​burst in two: one half fell to earth, and from it ‌come all the whetstone rocks in the world; the other half ‌drove into Thor's head, and he fell forward. But Mjǫllnir ​did not stop — it struck Hrungnir's head and crushed the ‌skull to small pieces, and the giant fell forward across ​Thor, his foot lying on Thor's neck. Þjálfi went at Mǫkkurkálfi, ​and the clay giant fell with little glory.

### The Foot No ‌God Could Lift (Skáldskaparmál 19)

Then the strangest aftermath in ‌the corpus: Thor lay pinned, and neither he nor Þjálfi could ‌shift the giant's foot from his neck. All the Æsir ‌came, when they learned, and together they could not lift it. ​At last came Magni, son of Thor and the giantess Járnsaxa ‌— three nights old — and threw Hrungnir's foot off ​his father, saying it was a pity he had come so ​late: he thought he would have struck the giant dead ​with his fist. Thor gave him Gullfaxi for the deed, and ‌Óðinn objected that he had given the fine horse to a ​giantess's son rather than to his own father. The hone ​stayed in Thor's head. The völva Gróa, wife of Aurvandill the ​Bold, came to sing it loose with her spells, and ‌the stone was already working free — until Thor, to please ​her, told how he had carried Aurvandill in a basket out ​of Jötunheimr, and how the man's frozen toe, broken off ​and thrown into the sky, became the star called Aurvandill's Toe. ‌Gróa rejoiced so greatly at the news that she forgot ​her spells; the hone stirs in Thor's head to this day. ‌Therefore, Snorri warns, whetstones must never be thrown across the floor.

### ​The Skaldic Witness (Haustlöng)

Snorri quotes his sources, and for ‌this myth the source is Þjóðólfr of Hvin's Haustlöng — a ​shield-poem composed in the early tenth century, among the oldest ‌mythological verse we have. Þjóðólfr tells the whole combat in dense ‌dróttkvætt: the 'defier of the gods' who rode to the fight, ​the earth shaking beneath the giant's host, the whetstone bitten ​from the hard stone of the heart, the hammer answering. That ​a skald within living memory of the Viking Age's pagan ​courts could assume his hearers knew the whetstone, the clay giant, ‌and the fall proves the story was not Snorri's construction: it ‌was already old, already fixed, already the standard account of ​the hardest fight Thor ever fought.

sources.citation: Þjóðólfr of Hvin, Haustlöng (the shield-poem's account of the Hrungnir combat, quoted in Skáldskaparmál).
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. Hrungnir, Gullfaxi, Grjótúnagarðar, hein.

syncretism.body:
Hrungnir ​resists the ‌usual syncretic ‌moves. Attempts ​to read ​him as ​a reflex ​of an ​Indo-European dragon-slaying ‌have been ​made — ​a stone-bodied ‌chaos-being struck ​down by ‌the thunderer's ​missile does ‌resemble the ​Vedic Vṛtra ​pattern — ​but the ​fit is ​partial, since ‌Hrungnir steals ​nothing, hoards ‌nothing, and ​threatens no ‌waters; scholars ​treat the ‌combat as ​a native ‌Norse contest-epic ​rather than ​an inherited ‌myth. His ‌truer company ‌is within ​the corpus ​itself: he ‌is one ​of the ​named great ‌fights of ​Þórr, standing ​between Geirrøðr, ‌killed by ​a thrown ‌glowing iron, ​and Hymir, ​fished with ​and nearly ​killed by ‌the sea. ‌The whetstone ​lodged in ‌Thor's head ​has been ​compared with ‌the embedded ‌weapons of ‌other mythologies ‌— the ​fragment that ‌will not ​come out ​— but ​no source ‌identifies a ​borrowing, and ​the handbooks ​register Hrungnir ‌as a ​distinctively Norse ​invention, a ​giant built ‌of the ​very landscape ‌the North ​knew: stone, ‌clay, and ​weather.[^1]

Within ‌the Norse ‌tradition, closely ​related names ​in the ​corpus include ​[[alfheimr|Álfheimr]], [[andvari|Andvari]], ‌[[angrboda|Angrboða]], [[audhumla|Auðhumla]], ‌[[baldr|Baldr]], and ​[[baugi|Baugi]].

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

cultural-legacy.body: Hrungnir's ​afterlife runs ‌through the ‌skalds before ​it runs ​through ​anyone else: ​Haustlöng made ​his fall ‌one ​of the ​foundation-texts of ‌Norse poetics, ​and Snorri ‌cites ​the poem ‌as the ​authority for ​the myth, ​so ​that every ​handbook of ‌Old Norse ​literature ‌meets him ​early. The ‌Victorians took ​up the ‌clay ​giant — ‌Mǫkkurkálfi recurs ​in retellings ​as ‌the archetype ‌of the ‌hollow colossus, ​all size ​and ‌mare's heart ​— and ​the detail ‌that whetstones ​must ​not be ‌thrown across ​the floor ‌survived ​in folklore ​collections as ​a curiosity ​of thunder-lore. ‌In ‌modern reception ​he is ‌the template ​for every ​stone-hearted ‌boss the ‌genre has ‌built since: ‌fantasy ​games and ‌novels cast ​his duel ​whenever a ​hero ‌must fight ​a mountain ​that can ​throw ‌back. His ​name never ​entered living ​use the ‌way ​Baldr's or ‌Thor's did; ​it remains ‌exactly what ​the ‌Edda made ‌it — ​the name ​of ​the strongest ​thing the ‌hammer ever ‌had to ​kill.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

archaeology.body: Hrungnir ​is a ‌textual figure: ‌no runestone ​invokes him, ​no votive ​deposit names ​him, and ​no picture ‌stone can ​be securely ​tied to ‌the duel ​— though ‌the tradition ​of ‌carving mythic ​combat on ​picture and ​rune stones ​is exactly ​the world ‌his skald ​belonged to. ‌His material ​witness is ‌instead a ​poem about ‌an object: ​Þjóðólfr ‌of Hvin's ​Haustlöng was ​composed for ‌a painted ‌shield, a ‌Viking-Age prestige ​object bearing ​mythic scenes, ‌and the ​verses Snorri ​quotes are ‌our evidence ​that the ​Hrungnir combat ‌belonged ​to that ‌visual repertoire ​in the ​early tenth ​century. The ​myth's own ‌materiality is ‌geological: Snorri ​anchors the ‌shattered whetstone ​in the ​landscape — ‌the hone-rocks ‌of the ‌world ‌are its ​debris — ‌and the ​taboo against ​throwing whetstones ​across the ‌floor entered ​Scandinavian folk ​custom as ​the myth's ‌trace in ​daily practice. ​The literary ​witnesses ‌hang by ​the usual ‌threads: Skáldskaparmál ​in the ‌Codex Regius ​of the ‌Prose Edda ‌and its ​sister manuscripts, ​and the ​Haustlöng stanzas ​preserved nowhere ‌else but ‌in Snorri's ​quotation.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

meditation.body: Hrungnir ​is the ‌Edda's essay ‌on confidence ​without flexibility. ​Every part ​of him ​is the ​hardest ‌available material ​— heart ​of stone, ‌head of ​stone, shield ‌of stone ​— and ‌the ​myth's arithmetic ​is that ​hardness is ​not the ​same as ‌strength. The ​whetstone is ‌the ​perfect weapon ‌for him: ​a stone ‌whose entire ​purpose is ‌to sharpen ​other things, ​hurled ‌once, shattering ‌on the ‌first iron ​it meets. ​Against him ‌the Edda ​sets two ​counter-images. ‌Mǫkkurkálfi, the ​engineered champion, ​enormous and ‌empty, a ​mare's heart ‌quaking in ​nine leagues ​of ​clay — ​the warning ‌about size ‌without courage. ​And Magni, ‌three nights ​old, lifting ​what ‌all the ‌gods together ‌could not ‌— the ​warning about ‌measuring strength ​by age, ​rank, ​or expectation. ‌Hrungnir wagered ​his head ​on a ​horse race ‌and lost ​it in ​a ​duel. The ‌name survives, ​etymology unknown, ‌as the ​corpus's permanent ‌reminder that ​being the ‌strongest ‌thing in ​the room ​is a ​wager too ​— and ‌someone always ‌holds the ​hammer.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda preserves Hrungnir in Old Norse alliterative verse. Poems such as Völuspá, Hávamál, and Grímnismál place Hrungnir within the cosmological drama of giant.

The meter encodes stress and alliteration that the normalized spelling Hrungnir attempts to carry forward into the digital record.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), trans. Anthony Faulkes.

prose-edda.body:
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda systematizes the myths of Hrungnir for a thirteenth-century Icelandic audience. Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál preserve genealogies, kennings, and narratives.

These sources frame Hrungnir as giant. The restoration Hrungnir keeps the Old Norse vowel length visible in the address bar.[^1]

runic-evidence.body:
Direct runic attestations of Hrungnir are not known in the surviving corpus; the name appears in medieval manuscripts rather than on rune stones. When reconstructed in Younger Futhark, the form underscores the distance between manuscript normalization and epigraphic habit.

PuniCodex displays the reconstructed runic form as the original script while noting the evidentiary gap honestly.[^1]

sagas.body:
Saga literature — family sagas, legendary sagas, and kings' sagas — keeps Hrungnir alive in prose narrative. The figure functions as giant in stories that blend history, genealogy, and myth.

The normalized name Hrungnir marks the scholarly form behind these later retellings.[^1]
